title: Research data, metadata, and the work of reuse
blurb: A field guide through Matthew Mayernik’s research interests: how scientific data become described, connected, credited, and sustained.

person.name: Matthew Mayernik
person.affiliation: NSF NCAR Library, University Corporation for Atmospheric Research
person.expertise: Research data curation, metadata practices and standards, data citation, and the institutions behind scientific information

notes.takeaway: Treats metadata as both a product and an activity, shaped by human and computational work.
notes.why: A foundation for examining how descriptions become evidence.

papers.title: Data Conservancy Provenance, Context, and Lineage Services: Key Components for Data Preservation and Curation

notes.takeaway: Connects provenance and contextual information across storage, archiving, preservation, and curation services.
notes.why: Keeping files is only one layer of preserving usable research.

papers.title: Research data and metadata curation as institutional issues

notes.takeaway: Explains variation in data practices through institutional norms, intermediaries, routines, standards, and material objects.
notes.why: Curation arrangements vary within organizations and disciplines, not just between them.

papers.title: The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship

notes.takeaway: Sets out findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reuse principles for human and machine use.
notes.why: A shared statement of goals against which specific implementations can be examined.

papers.title: Linking Publications and Data: Challenges, Trends, and Opportunities

notes.takeaway: Examines the technical and social work of creating and maintaining links between research articles and data.
notes.why: A link records a relationship, but may not explain why that relationship matters.

papers.title: Building Geoscience Semantic Web Applications Using Established Ontologies

notes.takeaway: Describes EarthCollab's reuse and integration of ontologies for geodesy and polar-science discovery.
notes.why: Shared vocabularies must be selected for actual users, systems, and questions.

papers.title: Assessing the uptake of persistent identifiers by research infrastructure users

notes.takeaway: Four case studies show growth in identifier-based references with different patterns across research resources.
notes.why: Assigning identifiers and changing citation behavior are distinct achievements.

notes.takeaway: Frames openness as continuing work shaped by researchers' accountabilities and the cost of making data understandable.
notes.why: Open-data policy needs to account for the labor and incentives of implementation.

papers.title: Metadata accounts: Achieving data and evidence in scientific research

notes.takeaway: Studies how scientists document, describe, annotate, organize, and manage data in everyday work.
notes.why: Observing practice reveals context that a required metadata form may miss.

notes.takeaway: Offers a framework and matrix for assessing threats to the continued use of scientific data.
notes.why: Preservation priorities need evidence about risks, resources, and responsibilities.

papers.title: Technical standards within socio-technical systems: An Annual Review of Information Science and Technology (ARIST) paper

notes.takeaway: Reviews standards as human-made artifacts that organize work and reflect social, economic, and political choices.
notes.why: Technical conformity alone does not explain how a standard works in practice.

papers.title: Scaling ORCID Adoption: Technical and Organizational Approaches Within a Research Organization

notes.takeaway: Reports UCAR's combination of outreach, profile analysis, software, and repository integration to expand ORCID use.
notes.why: Identity infrastructure requires continued organizational work alongside APIs.

sections.label: Foundations: data need context
sections.summary: Metadata describes how data can be interpreted, while curation preserves that context over time. Institutional studies explain why the necessary work depends on norms, routines, people, and resources.
questions: Who creates the context that later users need?

sections.label: Progression: linking the research record
sections.summary: FAIR principles, publication-data links, and reused ontologies create routes between research objects. They also expose choices about which relationships a system records and whose needs it serves.
questions: What scientific relationship does a link actually assert?

sections.label: Practice: studying what researchers actually do
sections.summary: Empirical studies of identifiers, openness, and metadata show how policies meet everyday research. Adoption is observable behavior, and useful descriptions take sustained work rather than a single deposit.
questions: Which changes in behavior show that a policy is working?

sections.label: Frontier: durable, accountable infrastructure
sections.summary: Risk assessment, critical studies of standards, and institutional identity projects broaden evaluation beyond technical compliance. The question is whether infrastructure remains usable and supported as people and systems change.
questions: Who maintains the record when a project or service ends?

opportunities: Study what users can discover, understand, cite, and reproduce, alongside whether metadata fields are populated.
Document who maintains identifiers, repairs descriptions, and supports users so that infrastructure budgets include this work.
practices: Connect each dataset to its methods, versions, contributors, and related outputs.
Pair technical integration with observation of user practices and ongoing maintenance.
